egypt.title: The Great Pyramid of Khufu
egypt.builders: Ancient Egyptian builders working for King Khufu
egypt.detail: Its outside was once covered with fine white limestone. Some of that stone arrived by boat.
egypt.story: About 4,600 years ago, Egyptian builders raised the Great Pyramid at Giza for King Khufu. It was a royal tomb. Teams worked together to cut, move, and fit huge stones. Most of the pyramid is limestone. Its outside once had a smooth covering of fine limestone, and boats brought some of this stone to the building site. The pyramid stood near the Nile valley, at the desert’s edge. Look at the photograph: many outer stones are now missing, so you can see the rougher blocks below!
egypt.simplification: Our small block model teaches layers and counting. The real pyramid had smooth sloping sides and far more stones. It is not an exact reconstruction.

maya.title: El Castillo: Temple of Kukulcán
maya.date: About 900–1200 CE (the city’s main building era)
maya.purpose: A temple raised on a stepped pyramid
maya.detail: The real pyramid has nine stepped levels and stairways on four sides.
maya.story: Maya builders made El Castillo in the city of Chichén Itzá, in what is now Mexico. The city’s main building era was about 900 to 1200 CE. This stepped pyramid supported a temple linked with Kukulcán, the Feathered Serpent. It has nine levels and stairways on all four sides. Near the spring and autumn equinoxes, sunlight and shadows can make a snake-like pattern beside a stairway. Imagine its busy ceremonial plaza, with people and buildings around it. Our little model helps you explore its layered shape.
maya.simplification: Our small terraces, temple assembly and stair flights teach planning and counting. Their size, colors, piece counts and arrangement are teaching choices, not an exact archaeological reconstruction.

mesopotamia.title: The Great Ziggurat of Ur
mesopotamia.purpose: A raised religious platform in the temple area of Nanna, the moon god
mesopotamia.detail: A surviving brick from Ur has a king’s inscription and a dog’s paw print!
mesopotamia.story: Around 2100 BCE, Sumerian builders worked for King Ur-Nammu at Ur, in what is now Iraq. They built a ziggurat: a huge stepped platform for a temple. It belonged to the sacred area of Nanna, the moon god. Builders used clay bricks in this river-plain city. Here is a tiny clue from their world: a brick from Ur still has a dog’s paw print, made before the clay dried! The ziggurat’s upper parts have not survived. The photograph shows the remaining structure, with restored lower parts.
mesopotamia.simplification: Our model teaches the idea of a stepped temple platform. The original upper stages are uncertain. Our small temple assembly, layers and piece count are imaginative teaching choices, not an exact reconstruction.
